name: Femi Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine by me. I'll give you the straight version.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Great. Could you walk me through a normal working day, start to finish?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the regional warehouse for a home improvement chain, out past the retail park. It's bulky stuff: kitchen units, doors, bags of plaster, decking boards. I pick orders onto pallets with an electric pallet truck, wrap them, label them for the store lorries or home delivery. Six till two, and some days it's 25 tonnes through my hands, near enough.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's physical and you can see what you've done, a full bay of wrapped pallets at the end. What wears me out is my back after a day of plasterboard, and that the pay hasn't moved much. My partner Hana works at a nursery, and between us we get by, but I've got less than a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say right, so the robots aren't coming for the decking boards after all. I'd joke about it at break. Online I'd maybe share a funny post, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job stays, and I stay on lower pay with no cushion. That's not nothing, it's still a worry, but it's a familiar one. The system already tells us what to pick, so a bit more AI in the office doesn't touch me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally do the counterbalance forklift licence, the company pays half and it's £1.20 an hour more once you're on the trucks. I'd try to put £50 a month away. And I'd keep using the AI thing now and then to check my payslip and holiday, because I got underpaid once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because the money's tight. But steady, I know where I stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you got underpaid once. What happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They missed my Sunday rate for three weeks. I put my payslip into the AI app and asked it to check the sums, then took that to the office. Got £84 back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Hana think about your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks I should push for team leader. I'm not sure I want the headache. I'd rather drive the forklift and go home on time.

say: I'd **joke at break** that robots aren't coming for the decking boards after all.
I'd maybe share a **funny post** online, nothing serious.
think: My job stays, but I stay on **lower pay** with no cushion.
More AI in the **office** doesn't touch me; the system already sets my picks.
do: Do the **counterbalance forklift** licence, half paid, for £1.20 an hour more.
Use an **AI app** now and then to check payslips and holiday.
feel: **Uneasy** because money is tight, but steady about where he stands.
S0.quote: I put my payslip into the AI app and asked it to check the sums, then took that to the office. Got £84 back.
fieldNote: He uses **AI** for small, concrete wins like a payslip check.
His plan is a modest step up: the **forklift licence**.
His partner pushes **team leader**; he'd rather go home on time.

steps.text: Get the counterbalance forklift licence with the company paying half
Check payslips with an AI app each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it'll hit the office first, the buyers and the people booking deliveries. I'd say bulky goods are hard for robots, which is true. I'd say keep calm and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think our planner and the transport booking go to software, and maybe a couple of the office team. Robots for kitchen units and wet plaster bags are a long way off, there's nothing standard about our stuff. I'd feel it later, not now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the forklift licence in the first six months. I'd ask for a go at the new warehouse system when they bring it in, because the people who understand it get kept. And I'd keep the £50 a month going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more for the office lot than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said bulky goods are hard for robots. What makes you so sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've seen the videos, they pick boxes off shelves. Try picking a 2.4 metre door that's been put back in the wrong bay with a pallet of tiles on top. I'm not sure, but I'd bet on a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra on transport bookings. She's been there twenty years and she's brilliant on the phone, but that's exactly the job a computer takes. I'd tell her to get in early on the new system.

say: I'd say the **office** goes first: buyers and delivery booking.
I'd say **bulky goods** are hard for robots, and keep calm.
think: Robots for **kitchen units** and plaster bags are a long way off.
I'd feel it **later**, not now; the planners feel it first.
do: Get the **forklift licence** in the first six months.
Volunteer to learn the **new warehouse system** early.
Keep the **£50 a month** savings going.
feel: **Uneasy**, more for the office staff than for himself.
S1.quote: Try picking a 2.4 metre door that's been put back in the wrong bay with a pallet of tiles on top.
fieldNote: Judges his own work as **hands-on and messy**, so later and less exposed.
Worries for **Sandra**, a long-serving transport booker.
Plans to be one of the people who **understand the system**.

steps.text: Pass the counterbalance forklift licence within six months
Volunteer to learn the new warehouse system early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the government, something sensible, not panic. Help for people retraining, help with rent. I'd say that at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AGI in 2028 means the office is gone and the whole warehouse runs off one system. Then 2031 the robots that can lift a door arrive, and my licence is worth nothing. I'd be 32 with no savings and Hana's wage alone doesn't pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the three years. I'd look at an electrician course or plumbing, something you do in people's houses, because robots in a warehouse come before robots in someone's loft. I'd cut the takeaways and the car finance if I can. And I'd sit down with Hana and work out what we can live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Properly. I'd feel like I was running out of road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why trades, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every house is different. A warehouse is the same every day, that's the point of a warehouse. I'd want something where the job is a bit of a puzzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can you afford a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not really. I'd need a funded one or an apprenticeship that pays. Even at £8 an hour as an apprentice, we'd be eating at Hana's mum's a lot.

say: I'd ask the **government** for a sensible plan, not panic.
I'd say people need help with **retraining and rent**.
think: By **2031** robots can lift a door, and my forklift licence is worth nothing.
At 32 with **no savings**, my partner's wage alone can't cover rent.
do: Use the **three-year gap** to start an electrician or plumbing course.
Cut **takeaways** and the car finance if possible.
Work out a **bare-minimum budget** with his partner.
feel: **Alarmed**, like he's running out of road.
S2.quote: A warehouse is the same every day, that's the point of a warehouse. I'd want something where the job is a bit of a puzzle.
fieldNote: He reads the **robot delay** clearly and spends it on a trade.
Can't afford a course unless it's **funded or paid**.
His reasoning is practical: **every house is different**.

steps.text: Start a funded electrician or plumbing apprenticeship
Cut takeaways and try to clear the car finance
Eat at his partner's mum's to stretch an apprentice wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so nobody should be caught out. I'd say get a trade if you can. That's the practical advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years to AGI, robots around 2034, I'd be 35. That's enough for a proper apprenticeship and a couple of years qualified before the warehouse goes. It's still a job loss, but one I can plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the forklift licence now for the extra money while it lasts. In year two I'd apply for an electrical apprenticeship, part time if they do it. I'd try to save £80 a month for the drop in pay when I switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but in control. It's a plan I could actually stick to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you switch earlier than year two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it would. I'm not one to move on a rumour. If they put robots in the bay next to me, that would shift me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mates on shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get a ticket for something. Forklift is fine for now, but get a trade ticket as well.

say: I'd call five years a **fair warning**, so nobody should be caught out.
I'd give the practical advice: **get a trade** if you can.
think: At **35** I'd have done an apprenticeship and a couple of qualified years.
It's still a **job loss**, but one I can plan around.
do: Get the **forklift licence** now for the extra pay while it lasts.
Apply for an **electrical apprenticeship** in year two.
Save **£80 a month** for the pay drop when switching.
feel: **Anxious but in control**: a plan he could stick to.
S3.quote: I'm not one to move on a rumour. If they put robots in the bay next to me, that would shift me.
fieldNote: Five years turns a cliff into a **sequence**: licence, then apprenticeship.
He'd move faster only if he **saw robots** in the next bay.
Advises mates to get a **trade ticket** too.

steps.text: Pass the forklift licence for the extra £1.20 an hour
Apply for an electrical apprenticeship in year two
Save £80 a month for the apprentice pay drop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so people should stop worrying and start planning. I'd say that to Hana and the lads. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years for AGI and robots around 2039. I'd be 40. Honestly, I might not even need to leave, I could be the forklift lead by then. But I'd want a trade anyway, because I don't want to be 40 and starting over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Forklift licence this year, team leader if it comes up, which would please Hana. An evening electrical course in a few years once I've got a bit saved. Keep the £50 a month going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the normal kind. Money's still tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you didn't want the team leader headache. What's changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time to stay on the floor. If I'm the team leader, I'm the one they keep to run the robots. That's worth a headache.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Hana wanted to move closer to her family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd go, probably. Her family's two hours away, and there's a big warehouse there too. I'm not tied to this place.

say: I'd tell people ten years is **plenty**: stop worrying and start planning.
I'd keep it **undramatic** with my partner and the lads.
think: I might not need to leave; I could be **forklift lead** by 2039.
I'd still want a **trade** so I'm not starting over at 40.
do: Go for **team leader** if it comes up.
Start an evening **electrical course** in a few years.
feel: **Uneasy** in the normal way, because money is still tight.
S4.quote: If I'm the team leader, I'm the one they keep to run the robots. That's worth a headache.
fieldNote: With a decade he **changes his mind** about team leader.
Willing to **move** two hours to his partner's family.
**Money** is still the main background worry.

steps.text: Pass the forklift licence this year
Apply for team leader when the post comes up
Move near his partner's family if she wants to

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Three years to a robot that can lift a door is not a lot when you've got no savings. What would help is a paid apprenticeship for people my age, not just school leavers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about our backs. A lot of us won't last to 2039 anyway, the plasterboard does for your back. Some people might be glad of a robot doing the heavy lifting.

headlineQuote: A lot of us won't last to 2039 anyway, the plasterboard does for your back. Some people might be glad of a robot doing the heavy lifting.
portrait: **Femi** is 27 and picks **bulky goods** at a home improvement warehouse, living with his partner, a nursery worker.
He has less than a month saved and uses **AI** now and then, once to win back £84 of pay.
He's **pragmatic** and moves once he's seen proof, starting with a forklift licence.
He plans a move into a **trade** when the timeline is short.
He goes from uneasy to **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, then back to uneasy with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years to robots is short with no **savings**.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** open to people his age, not only school leavers.
